section.title: I Give You Thanks with My Whole Heart
section.sectionRationale: The first of the eight closing Davidic psalms that gather Book V toward its finale, this individual thanksgiving pairs personal gratitude for answered prayer with a vision of kings of the earth one day praising the LORD, David's confidence resting not on his own strength but on God's exalted name and word.
section.thesis: David's wholehearted thanksgiving for a prayer already answered opens into confidence that the LORD who exalts His name and word above all things will finish the work He has begun, a pattern of praise, humility, and settled trust fulfilled in Christ, before whom every king will one day bow.
section.frameNote: Three movements: wholehearted thanksgiving before every power for an answered prayer, verses 1-3; the LORD's exalted name reaching the kings of the earth even as He stoops to the lowly, verses 4-6; and confidence that He will finish what He has begun, verses 7-8.

units.label: Wholehearted thanks for an answered prayer

verses.text: I give You thanks with all my heart; before the gods I sing Your praises.
I bow down toward Your holy temple and give thanks to Your name for Your {{chesed|loving devotion}} and Your faithfulness; You have exalted Your name and Your word above all else.
On the day I called, You answered me; You emboldened me and strengthened my soul.

units.label: The LORD's name reaches the kings of the earth
units.note: high, yet near to the lowly

verses.text: All the kings of the earth will give You thanks, O LORD, when they hear the words of Your mouth.
They will sing of the ways of the LORD, for the glory of the LORD is great.
Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the {{shaphal|lowly}}; but the proud He knows from afar.

units.label: Confidence He will finish His purpose

verses.text: If I walk in the midst of trouble, You preserve me from the anger of my foes; You extend Your hand, and Your right hand saves me.
The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me. O LORD, Your loving devotion endures forever, do not abandon the works of Your hands.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion, God's loyal love that does not quit. David thanks God for chesed paired with faithfulness, the two words that most often summarize the LORD's covenant character, Exodus 34:6.

shaphal.gloss: Low, humble, brought down. God's high exaltation does not distance Him from the lowly; instead He draws near to them, while keeping the proud at a distance, a pattern echoed throughout Scripture, Isaiah 57:15, James 4:6.

basic.context: David gives thanks for a specific answered prayer, likely a victory that drew the attention of surrounding kings, and grounds his gratitude not in the outcome itself but in the character of the God who answered, whose name and word He has exalted above everything else.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, specific thanksgiving for an actual answered prayer, yet its logic generalizes: because God has proven faithful once, He can be trusted to finish what He has started. The psalm describes David's own experience; it prescribes a pattern of grounding present confidence in past answered prayer.
basic.originalLanguages: David thanks God for His chesed, steadfast covenant love, paired with faithfulness, the classic pairing that summarizes the LORD's character since Exodus 34:6. Though high above all, God attends to the shaphal, the lowly, while keeping His distance from the proud, a reversal of worldly power that runs through both Testaments.
basic.typology: The vision of all the kings of the earth giving God thanks, verse 4, anticipates the day every knee bows to Jesus, Philippians 2:10-11, and the nations streaming to worship in the new creation, Revelation 21:24.
basic.christ: David's confidence that the LORD will fulfill His purpose for him, verse 8, is fulfilled supremely in Christ, who declared on the cross, It is finished, John 19:30, and who, though exalted above all, drew near to the lowly throughout His earthly ministry, Matthew 11:29, Philippians 2:6-8.
basic.god: God is shown as exalted above every rival power, yet personally attentive, answering prayer the very day it is offered, drawing near to the humble, and faithfully finishing the work He begins in those who are His.
basic.crossReferences: Philippians 1:6 echoes verse 8's confidence that God will complete His good work. Philippians 2:9-11 fulfills the vision of every king giving God thanks. James 4:6 restates the LORD's nearness to the humble and distance from the proud. John 19:30 is the ultimate fulfillment of the LORD finishing His purpose.
basic.oneStory: David's thanksgiving for an answered prayer becomes confidence that the God who is high above all, yet near to the lowly, will finish what He has begun, a pattern completed in Christ, before whom every king will one day give thanks and in whom God's saving purpose is finished forever.

context.literary:
Psalm 138 stands at the head of the last Davidic collection in the Psalter, Psalms 138 to 145, and it reads like a deliberate answer to what came just before. Psalm 137 is the cry of exiles who cannot sing by the rivers of Babylon. Psalm 138 begins with a man who sings with all his heart, and the very first verb, 'I give You thanks,' is the verb of public praise. The Songs of Ascents and the Hallel psalms are behind us, and a new run of David's own prayers begins.

The psalm is built in three movements of unequal length. Verses 1 to 3 are personal thanks in the first person, ending on the testimony of verse 3, 'On the day I called, You answered me.' Verses 4 to 6 widen to the world: all the kings of the earth give thanks, they sing of the ways of the LORD, and they learn that the high God stoops to the lowly. Verses 7 and 8 return to the single believer and look ahead, with 'If I walk in the midst of trouble' and 'The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me.' The movement is from memory, to the nations, to the future, and it turns on the hinge of God's faithfulness.

Covenant love frames the whole poem. 'Your loving devotion' stands in the central praise of verse 2 and closes the whole psalm in verse 8. That inclusio of covenant love around the poem tells the reader what it is really about. Everything between is an illustration of that love in action: answering, strengthening, exalting the lowly, preserving in trouble.

The psalm also plays with height and distance. God's name is exalted 'above all else,' verse 2. He is 'on high,' verse 6, yet He attends to the lowly. The proud He knows 'from afar,' the same word used in Psalm 139:2 of God's knowledge of thoughts. The nearer a person comes in humility, the closer God is, and the more a person lifts himself up, the more distant he finds God. Verse 8 closes with a petition, the only real request in the psalm, and it is a request for finishing, not for starting.
context.historical:
The title says only 'Of David,' and the content fits what the books of Samuel tell about his reign. After God's covenant promise in 2 Samuel 7, David prayed that God would confirm the word He had spoken, 2 Samuel 7:25. Chapter 8 then lists victory after victory over the Philistines, Moabites, Arameans and Edomites, and 2 Samuel 8:14 summarises that 'the LORD gave David victory wherever he went.' A king who had been hunted by Saul and had lived in caves now had neighbouring kings paying tribute and watching what his God could do. Verse 4's picture of kings hearing 'the words of Your mouth' reads naturally against that background.

The phrase 'before the gods,' verse 1, would have made sense in a world where every nation had its own deities and a king's victories were credited to them. David sings in the presence of those claimed powers, as a deliberate act of witness, that the LORD alone had answered him. Whether the 'gods' are the pagan deities, heavenly beings, or earthly rulers is a question taken up below, but in each case the first hearers would have heard a public confession in a hostile or competitive setting.

'I bow down toward Your holy temple,' verse 2, needs care. Solomon's temple did not yet exist in David's lifetime. The Hebrew word is the one that can mean a palace or a sanctuary, and it is used of the tent shrine at Shiloh in 1 Samuel 1:9 and 3:3. David may mean the tent he had pitched for the ark in Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 6:17, or he may be using the word for the sanctuary as God's house in the wider sense. Later generations of Israelites in exile prayed 'toward' that place, as Solomon had asked in 1 Kings 8:29 and 8:44, and Daniel did it in Babylon, Daniel 6:10. The psalm was therefore easy to take up in exile, and its placement after Psalm 137 may reflect that use.

The social world of the 'lowly' and 'the proud' is also historical. In the ancient Near East power was displayed by monuments and tribute, and a king who attended to the lowly was unusual. David's God is not a patron of the powerful.
context.canonical:
The psalm draws on the oldest stratum of Israel's confession. 'Loving devotion and faithfulness' in verse 2 is the pair that God Himself announced to Moses, Exodus 34:6, and that the rest of the Psalter repeats. The language of verse 3, calling and being answered, belongs to the deepest memory of the exodus, when Israel cried out and God heard, Exodus 2:23-25. David then uses the same grammar of covenant for his own story.

The vision of verses 4 and 5, kings of the earth singing the ways of the LORD, belongs to a thread that runs from the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, to the royal Psalms where the nations bow to David's heir, Psalm 2:10-12 and Psalm 72:11. Isaiah develops it: kings will shut their mouths at the Servant, Isaiah 52:15, and kings will come to the brightness of Zion's rising, Isaiah 60:3. The last chapters of Revelation see the end of that road, where 'the kings of the earth will bring their glory' into the city, Revelation 21:24.

Verse 6 is a short summary of what the Old Testament says about God's character toward the humble. Isaiah 57:15 has the high and holy One dwelling with the contrite, and Isaiah 66:2 has Him esteeming the one who trembles at His word. Proverbs 3:34 gives the pairing of grace to the humble and opposition to the proud, which James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 then quote. Mary's song uses the same movement when she says God has 'exalted the humble,' Luke 1:52.

Verse 8's confidence recalls Philippians 1:6, which uses the language of a work begun and carried to completion. The New Testament does not quote Psalm 138 by name, but its themes are so much taken up that the psalm reads like a first draft of several New Testament doctrines: the exaltation of the Name, the nations' homage, and the perseverance of those God has begun to save.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted Israel, and the nations listening, to see that gratitude is a form of testimony. He does not thank God in private; he sings 'before the gods,' in front of every power that might claim credit. The psalm asks the worshiper to say publicly what God has done, and to say it with all the heart rather than a part of it.

He also meant to teach where trust rests. The reason David is confident about the future is not his strength, his army or his past success. It is the character of God, His 'loving devotion and faithfulness,' and the fact that God has put His own name and word on the line, verse 2. A person who has asked and been answered has a reason to ask again.

The third purpose is humbling. The same psalm that opens with a king's victory ends with a prayer that God not 'abandon the works of Your hands,' verse 8. The victor knows he is still a work in progress, and that the finishing belongs to God. First hearers were meant to leave the psalm thankful, unafraid of the next trouble, and unwilling to give any credit to their own pride, since the proud are kept at a distance.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's own experience of one specific answered prayer, probably a time of national success. It does not promise that every prayer will be answered on the same day, and verse 3 should not be read as a rule that God always acts at once. Other psalms, such as Psalm 13 and Psalm 22, show believers waiting and crying in the dark, and they are just as much Scripture.

What the psalm prescribes is a pattern of life. Give thanks with the whole heart. Say so in front of others. Rest present confidence on past faithfulness. Look to God's character before looking at circumstances. Believe that the one who has begun a work in you will finish it, which Paul says in his own way in Philippians 1:6.

The claim of verse 8 also needs a careful reading. 'The LORD will fulfill His purpose for me' is not a promise of comfort or success. It is a promise that God will complete what He has set out to do, which in the New Testament includes shaping believers into the likeness of Christ, Romans 8:28-29. The 'works of Your hands' are the people God made and saved, and the petition asks God to be true to Himself.

debates.question: Who are 'the gods' in verse 1?

views.label: Pagan deities
views.case: The Hebrew word elohim is the ordinary word for the gods of the nations, and David's victories over neighbouring peoples are the natural setting. Psalm 97:7 calls on 'all you gods' to worship the LORD in the same way, and the verse then reads as a defiant act of witness in the face of rival claims.

views.label: Heavenly beings
views.case: Elohim can also name members of God's heavenly court, as in Psalm 82:1 and Psalm 29:1. The Greek translation of this psalm reads 'before angels,' and many Jewish and Christian readers have followed that line, hearing a song sung in the presence of the heavenly assembly.

views.label: Earthly rulers
views.case: Verse 4 speaks of 'the kings of the earth,' and elohim is sometimes used of judges and rulers, as in Psalm 82:6. On this view the psalm pictures David singing before the kings of the nations and so anticipates what verse 4 promises.

debates.bearing: All three readings end in the same place: David refuses to keep his thanks private, and he does it in front of every power that might claim credit. The reader should prefer the one that fits the immediate context, probably rival gods or rulers, without needing to settle it to hear the point.

debates.question: What does it mean that God exalted His name and word 'above all else' in verse 2?

views.label: God's word surpasses even His name
views.case: Read literally, the line says that God has magnified His word above all His name. This would mean God's promises carry a weight greater than His reputation, because He has bound Himself to them. The covenant promise to David in 2 Samuel 7 would be the great example.

views.label: God has made His name and word known above every other thing
views.case: The BSB's 'above all else' takes the sense that nothing in all creation surpasses the name and the word. This fits Psalm 148:13, 'His name alone is exalted,' and the context of defeating rivals. The line is a doxology rather than a ranking.

views.label: God's acts have fulfilled His word and so vindicated His name
views.case: On this reading the exaltation is shown by the answered prayer of verse 3: the word spoken in promise has been kept in history, and the name has been honoured in the sight of nations.

debates.bearing: The Hebrew is compressed and translators differ, so no reading should be pressed into a rule. All three insist that God's name and God's word are tied together, and that the answer David received was a vindication of both.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 sets 'with all my heart' beside 'before the gods.' The verb 'give thanks,' yadah, is the verb of public confession. It is built from the word for 'hand' and carries the sense of acknowledging aloud, and the same verb is used of confessing sin in Leviticus 5:5 and of praising in Psalm 107:1. In both uses the speaker says openly what is true. The related noun, todah, is the name of the thank offering in Leviticus 7:12, so the psalm sets thanksgiving in the sanctuary as well as in the mouth.

Verse 2 uses 'bow down,' the verb that can mean fall flat in homage, with 'toward Your holy temple.' The preposition matters. David bows toward a place without claiming that God is confined to it, a nuance later Israel relied on when Solomon asked God to hear prayer offered toward the temple, 1 Kings 8:29-30. The 'loving devotion and faithfulness' are chesed and emet, the pairing of Exodus 34:6. Chesed is covenant loyalty, love that keeps a promise, and emet, from the root meaning to be firm, is dependable truth. Together they say that God's love is reliable because His truth does not change.

Verse 3 has a word of unusual force. 'You emboldened me' translates the verb that comes from the root rahav, meaning to be wide or large, and the BSB footnote gives 'You emboldened me with strength in my soul.' The picture is of a person stretched out and made roomy inside, enlarged where fear had squeezed. The word 'strength,' oz, is a major word for power, and it is joined to 'soul,' nephesh, so the strengthening is deep, not a mere cheer. The answer to prayer came as courage within.

In verse 6 'attends to' is the verb that normally means 'see.' God 'sees' the lowly, and in the Old Testament God's seeing is rarely passive. In Exodus 3:7 He sees the affliction of His people and comes down. The 'lowly,' shaphal, is the word for what is low and is set in contrast to 'on high,' ram. The 'proud' is gavoah, literally 'high,' so the pride is a self-exaltation that puts a person at the wrong altitude. God 'knows' the proud 'from afar,' meaning He keeps them at a distance, a use of 'know' that is not mere awareness but relationship.

In verse 8 'fulfill' translates a verb, gamar, meaning to bring to an end, to complete. Psalm 57:2 uses the same verb for 'God who fulfills His purpose for me,' so David is repeating a familiar confession. The 'works of Your hands' are the people God has made, and the plea 'do not abandon' uses a verb of letting go, as if of a grip. Paul's 'carry it on to completion' in Philippians 1:6 lives in the same world of ideas.

typology.type: David's victories over the kings of the nations, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: David's wars in 2 Samuel 8 made the surrounding kings subjects and tribute payers, and the psalm imagines them going further and giving thanks to the LORD. The correspondence is with Christ the greater David, to whom the nations belong by the Father's gift, Psalm 2:8, and before whom the kings of the earth will bring their glory, Revelation 21:24. The escalation is from forced tribute to willing worship. The type falls short because David's conquests were by sword and left enemies bitter, while Christ's reign wins hearts through His own death, John 12:32.

typology.type: The holy temple toward which David bows, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: David bows toward the sanctuary where God's name dwelt, as Israel was taught to pray toward that place, 1 Kings 8:30. Jesus speaks of His own body as the temple, John 2:19-21, and tells the Samaritan woman that true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, John 4:21-24. The escalation is from a place to a Person, so that believers no longer face a building but come through Christ. The type falls short because the temple could be defiled and destroyed, while Christ's body was raised and cannot be.

typology.type: God exalting His name above all else, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: In the psalm God's name is exalted over all rivals. Paul says that God exalted Christ 'to the highest place' and gave Him 'the name above all names,' Philippians 2:9. The name of the LORD David honoured is now confessed at the name of Jesus, and every knee bows, Philippians 2:10-11. The escalation is that the exaltation comes after humiliation, through the obedience of the cross. The correspondence is not a claim that Psalm 138 speaks of Christ directly; it is a link of theme, and the type falls short in that David's exaltation was shared by no one else.

typology.type: The high God who attends to the lowly, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: Mary sings of the Lord who looks on the humble and exalts them, Luke 1:48 and 1:52, and the Son whom she carries is the great example. He was born in a stable and announced to shepherds, Luke 2:8-12, and He says, 'I am gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29. Paul writes that He 'humbled Himself' even to death on a cross, Philippians 2:8. The escalation is from God looking down at the lowly to God becoming one of them. The type is incomplete in the psalm because it stays at a distance of observation.

study.christ:
Psalm 138 does not speak of the Messiah by name, and it is better not to pretend it does. The links to Christ come in three ways: by pattern in David's story, by theme in the psalm's confession about God, and by the fulfilment of the hope David expressed in verse 8.

The first is the pattern of the king who is answered and then draws the nations. David's prayer after God's covenant promise, 2 Samuel 7:18-29, asks God to confirm His word forever, and the psalm gives thanks that He has done so. The seed promised in that covenant is, in the New Testament, Jesus, 'the Son of David,' Matthew 1:1 and Luke 1:32-33, and the nations' homage David hoped for belongs to His reign. Isaiah had foreseen kings shutting their mouths before the Servant, Isaiah 52:15, and Paul sees every tongue confessing Jesus as Lord, Philippians 2:11. Verse 4, 'when they hear the words of Your mouth,' becomes the gospel's pattern: the nations come to worship because the word has been proclaimed, Romans 10:17.

The second is the theme of the exalted God who stoops. Jesus is the picture of verse 6 made flesh. Although 'in the form of God,' He took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7. He sought out the lowly, tax collectors and sinners, the poor and the sick, and said the kingdom belonged to them, Luke 6:20. The proud, as the psalm says, are kept at a distance, and Jesus said it of the Pharisee and the tax collector in Luke 18:9-14, where the one who humbles himself goes home justified. The psalm's 'He attends to the lowly' is the gospel in small.

The third is verse 8. David asks God not to abandon the works of His hands. The cry of Jesus on the cross, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' Matthew 27:46, reverses that prayer: Christ was abandoned so that no believer will be. His final word, 'It is finished,' John 19:30, uses a verb for completion of a task, and it points to the accomplishing of the purpose God had for Him and, through Him, for His people. Because He finished the work, Paul can say with confidence that the one who began a good work in believers will carry it to completion, Philippians 1:6.

A caution keeps this honest. David's gratitude is for a particular answer in his own life, and the psalm should not be turned into a prediction of Calvary. What the psalm supplies is the language and logic of trust, a God whose steadfast love endures, and the New Testament shows where that love finally proved itself.
study.god:
The psalm gives a rounded picture of God, and the first note is that He is answerable to His own word. David's praise rests on two things God has put on the line, His name and His word, verse 2. A God who has bound Himself to what He says is a God whose character can be trusted in the dark. The psalm celebrates that He has acted in line with it.

He is the God who answers, and the speed is notable: 'On the day I called, You answered me,' verse 3. This does not mean every answer arrives at once, but that He is attentive, not remote. What He gives is not only deliverance from enemies but courage within, 'You emboldened me and strengthened my soul.' The first work of God in trouble is often in the person, not in the circumstance.

He is exalted and near at once, which is one of the great tensions of the doctrine of God. 'Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly,' verse 6. Scripture refuses to choose between transcendence and nearness. Isaiah sets the same pair in a single verse when the high and holy One dwells with the contrite, Isaiah 57:15. His height does not make Him indifferent, and His nearness does not make Him small. The proud, who stretch toward His level, find themselves farther away.

He is the God of all nations. The psalm imagines kings from everywhere hearing 'the words of Your mouth' and singing 'the ways of the LORD,' verses 4 and 5. The God of Israel is not a tribal deity. His word goes out to the world and His glory is 'great.' That is a theme that will carry through the rest of the Bible until Revelation.

He is a protector in trouble: 'If I walk in the midst of trouble, You preserve me,' verse 7. The wording is realistic, since the psalm expects to walk in trouble, not around it. God's hand and right hand are both put forward, one to shield and one to save.

He is faithful to finish. Verse 8 rests on the endurance of His loving devotion, and the request that He not abandon His handiwork shows that the believer's security is in God's commitment, not in his own grip. For worship, the psalm teaches that thanksgiving should be wholehearted, public, based on the character of God and not merely the gift, and open toward the future, since the God who has answered once is the God who will bring His work to its end.

crossReferences.note: The LORD announces His own name to Moses as compassionate and gracious, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness. Psalm 138:2 uses the same pair, chesed and emet, as the reason for thanks. David is not inventing a theology; he is repeating what God said about Himself at Sinai.

David's prayer after the covenant promise asks God to confirm His word forever so that His name will be magnified. Psalm 138:2 and 138:8 give the thanks and the continuing request. The psalm reads as the reflection of a man who has seen the word kept and asks for it to keep being kept.

David cries to 'God who fulfills His purpose for me' and sees God send forth His loving devotion and truth. It uses the same verb as Psalm 138:8 for God's completing work, and the same pair of covenant love and truth. The two psalms show the same confidence from two points in David's life.

The LORD is exalted over all the nations yet humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth, raising the poor from the dust. It states at greater length the balance Psalm 138:6 sets in one line: high above, yet close to the low. Each psalm uses the contrast to praise God.

The high and lofty One who inhabits eternity also dwells with the contrite and humble in spirit. This is the prophetic version of Psalm 138:6, showing that it is a settled part of Israel's theology that height and nearness belong together in God.

God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. James quotes Proverbs 3:34 and brings the same truth as Psalm 138:6 into the life of the church. The proud are kept far away while the lowly receive attention and help.

Mary's song celebrates God looking on the humble state of His servant and bringing down rulers while exalting the humble. It moves in the pattern of Psalm 138:6 and applies it to the coming of the Messiah, whom she carries.

God exalted Jesus to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names, so that every knee should bow. This is the large fulfilment of the hope of Psalm 138:2 and 138:4, that God's name would be exalted and the nations would acknowledge Him.

Paul is confident that He who began a good work will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. It restates the confidence of Psalm 138:8 as a promise to every believer, grounded now in Christ's finished work.

The nations will fear the name of the LORD and all the kings of the earth will fear His glory. Like Psalm 138:4-5 it looks beyond Israel to the kings of the earth honouring God. Both texts are part of the Psalter's steady expectation that God's rule will be acknowledged worldwide.

study.oneStory:
The psalm sits inside a larger story of a God who makes a name for Himself among the nations. After the flood and Babel, God called Abraham so that all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3. From that point every answered prayer and every victory is a small piece of that purpose. David's thanks in the presence of the 'gods' belongs there: a small king in a small land gives public thanks for a faithful God and imagines the world doing the same.

It also looks back to creation and the fall. In Genesis the proud were scattered and the humble received grace, from Cain's exile to Babel's tower, and the psalm says outright that the proud are known 'from afar,' verse 6. That is not new. From the first sin the human instinct has been to climb toward God's seat, Genesis 3:5, and the way back is by coming down, which is why Scripture keeps blessing the humble and the poor in spirit.

Ahead of the psalm lies David's own history, then the exile, in which Israel prayed toward the temple and found God still near. The psalm's vision of the kings giving thanks was only partially fulfilled in Solomon's day, when the queen of Sheba and kings came to hear his wisdom, 1 Kings 10:23-24. The full fulfilment waits for the descendant of David who is also David's Lord.

In Christ the psalm's hopes land. The God who is on high came down, He was answered on the third day, and God gave Him the name above all names. The nations now hear the words of His mouth and sing the ways of the LORD in every language, Revelation 7:9-10. The believer's confidence in verse 8 is anchored in His completed work, not in his own grip, and the apostle Paul builds on it in Philippians 1:6 and Romans 8:30.

The end of the story is the city in which the kings of the earth bring their glory, Revelation 21:24, and God's people see His face, Revelation 22:4. Everything the psalm hoped for, the great name, the song of the nations, the lowly attended to, the works of His hands brought to their finish, is gathered there, and the loving devotion that 'endures forever' has no more need of petition.

sermon.title: Above All Things
sermon.why: Begg expounds Psalm 138:2's declaration that God has exalted His name and word above all things, explaining how God's self-revelation through creation, conscience, His Word, and His Son strips away pride and leads to praise, directly serving this psalm's opening confession.

quiz.q: What specifically prompts David's thanksgiving in verses 1-3?

options.text: A prayer he called out that the LORD answered, emboldening and strengthening his soul on that very day.
options.note: Verse 3 ties the thanksgiving directly to a specific answered prayer.

options.text: A general feeling of gratitude with no particular cause.
options.note: The text specifies a concrete answered prayer, not a vague mood of thankfulness.

options.text: The building of a new temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: David bows toward the temple in worship, but the specific cause of thanksgiving is an answered prayer, not a construction project.

options.text: A treaty signed with a foreign king.
options.note: The psalm implies recognition by foreign kings will follow, verse 4, but the immediate cause of thanks is God's answer to prayer.

quiz.q: What has God exalted above all else, according to verse 2?

options.text: His name and His word.
options.note: Verse 2 states plainly that God has exalted His name and His word above all else.

options.text: The wealth and armies of Israel.
options.note: The text exalts God's name and word, not Israel's military or material strength.

options.text: The temple building itself above the LORD's own character.
options.note: David bows toward the temple, but what is exalted above all is God's name and word, not the structure.

options.text: David's own kingship over other nations.
options.note: The psalm's focus is God's self-revelation and character, not David's political standing.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe God's relationship to the lowly and the proud in verse 6?

options.text: Though the LORD is on high, He attends to the lowly, but the proud He knows from afar.
options.note: This exact reversal, God's nearness to the humble and distance from the proud, is the verse's central claim.

options.text: God treats the lowly and the proud in exactly the same way.
options.note: The verse draws a clear distinction; God draws near the lowly and distances the proud.

options.text: God ignores both the lowly and the proud equally.
options.note: The verse says God attends to the lowly, the opposite of ignoring them.

options.text: God rewards the proud for their confidence and achievement.
options.note: The verse says the opposite, that God knows the proud only from a distance.

quiz.q: What confidence does David express in verse 8 about God's purpose for him?

options.text: That the LORD will fulfill His purpose for him and asks God not to abandon the work of His own hands.
options.note: Verse 8 states this confidence directly, grounding it in God's enduring loving devotion.

options.text: That David must complete his own purpose entirely through his own effort.
options.note: The verse credits the LORD, not David's own effort, with fulfilling His purpose.

options.text: That David's troubles are now permanently over.
options.note: Verse 7 assumes ongoing trouble; the confidence is about God's preserving and completing work within it, not the absence of trouble.

options.text: That future generations will have to finish what David could not.
options.note: The verse expresses confidence in God's own faithfulness to finish the work, not a deferral to later generations.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's vision of kings giving God thanks connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates every knee bowing to Jesus and every tongue confessing Him as Lord.
options.note: Philippians 2:10-11 fulfills the psalm's picture of universal acknowledgment of God's supremacy.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament at all.
options.note: The psalm's vision of universal praise is directly picked up in passages like Philippians 2 and Revelation 21.

options.text: It predicts a specific political alliance in the first century.
options.note: The psalm speaks of ultimate worship and acknowledgment of God, not a particular historical treaty.

options.text: It is fulfilled only by the physical conquest of foreign kings by Israel's armies.
options.note: The fulfillment is worship and acknowledgment of God's greatness, not military conquest, culminating in Christ's universal lordship.

questions: David thanks God wholeheartedly for one specific answered prayer. What has God done for you recently that deserves the same wholehearted thanks?
David exalts God's name and word above everything else. What competes for that place of highest exaltation in your life right now?
God draws near to the lowly and keeps the proud at a distance. Where is pride keeping you at a distance from God's nearness this week?
David trusts that the LORD will finish the purpose He has begun, even amid ongoing trouble. What unfinished situation in your life needs that same confidence today?
This psalm anticipates kings of the earth one day giving God thanks, fulfilled in Christ before whom every knee will bow. How does that future certainty shape how you live now?

translationNotes.note: Before the gods can refer either to heavenly beings in God's court, as in Psalm 82:1, or ironically to the false gods of the nations; either reading exalts the LORD above every rival power.
You emboldened me and strengthened my soul carries a footnote possibility, You emboldened me with strength in my soul, both readings pointing to inward courage granted the day David called.
The two clauses, Your loving devotion endures forever and do not abandon the works of Your hands, read as a single flowing petition grounded in God's enduring covenant love.
